title: Learning to Align Question and Answer Utterances in Customer Service Conversation with Recurrent Pointer Networks
research_question: Can recurrent pointer-network models align each customer-service answer utterance with zero, one, or multiple preceding customer question utterances while exploiting conversational context and dependencies among alignments?
methodology: The authors sampled 10,000 human-to-human customer-service conversations and had five annotators mark which preceding customer utterances each server utterance answered, followed by additional review of inconsistent cases, yielding 5,741 labeled conversations. They formulated alignment from each server utterance to preceding customer utterances and developed two recurrent pointer-network architectures using utterance encoders, conversation encoders, and either shared or role-specific customer/server encoders. Classification and regression objectives were compared, with the regression formulation intended to handle multiple alignments without a tuned multi-label threshold. Data were split 80/10/10 for training, validation, and testing, and systems were evaluated with micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1.

key_findings.finding: The empirical data contain substantial non-bijective structure: None alignments account for 57% of answer utterances and One-to-Many alignments account for 12%, while an answered server utterance aligns to 1.38 customer questions on average when None cases are excluded.
The strongest reported RPN configuration, Model-II with regression loss, obtained overall precision 84.22%, recall 85.51%, and F1 84.86%, compared with F1 79.5% for the SHCNN+CISIR comparison system.
Model-II with regression loss achieved F1 94.07% on Empty alignments, exceeding the 91.1% F1 of the discriminative comparison system highlighted by the authors.
For One-to-Many cases, Model-II with regression loss achieved precision 91.51%, recall 71.67%, and F1 80.39%, compared with F1 76.27% for SHCNN+CISIR.

Regression loss handled One-to-Many alignment better than the classification formulation in Model-II, with F1 80.39% versus 76.38%, which the authors attribute to avoiding a difficult conversation-dependent threshold.
One-to-Many alignment remained harder than One-to-One alignment for the strongest model, with F1 80.39% versus 85.40% and notably lower recall.

limitations: The dataset is drawn from an in-house customer-service application, so external-domain and cross-organizational generalization is not established.
The task is restricted primarily to two-party customer-to-server question-answer direction; server questions to customers are discussed as a reversible extension rather than evaluated directly.
The unit of alignment is a whole utterance, so a single utterance containing several propositions cannot represent that only some propositions were answered.

Although a question with no incoming alignment could be inferred as unanswered, the model and evaluation are answer-centric and do not directly evaluate unanswered customer questions as a separate phenomenon.
The reported Fleiss' kappa of 0.523 indicates only moderate annotator agreement despite subsequent review.
The authors identify long conversational context as difficult for annotators and as an unresolved challenge.
Manual labeling is labor intensive, and unsupervised or semi-supervised alignment is left for future work.
The paper states that data and code would be shared with the academic community but does not provide a concrete release link in the paper.
raw_claims: The final annotated corpus contains 5,741 customer-service conversations.
Each server utterance is aligned only to earlier customer utterances in the main task formulation.
A server utterance that answers no customer question is assigned a None alignment.
More than half of the server utterances in the annotated data have None alignment.
Twelve percent of the alignments are One-to-Many cases.
Customers can ask several questions together and servers can answer them in a different order.
Delayed answers make simple nearest-utterance alignment unreliable.
One answer may correspond to several customer utterances expressing the same intention.
Conversation-level context and dependencies among different alignment decisions improve performance over pairwise content matching.
The regression RPN performs better than the classification variant on One-to-Many cases.
The proposed system does not decompose an utterance into individual propositions or subquestions.
